div.p: Window-Constrained Scheduling is one of the task models proposed in recent years for scheduling periodic realtime tasks where service must be guaranteed in only a fraction of the periods. In RTSS'2000, a Dynamic Window-Constrained Scheduling (DWCS) algorithm was proposed by West and Poellabauer [I71 for multiplexing multiple packet streams where the number of consecutive packet lost must be bounded. In this papel; we show that the DWCS algorithm can fail for arbitrarily low aggregate utilization rates of the packet streams. We shall show that Window-Constrained Scheduling is NP-hard in the strong sense. However if the execution time of all jobs is of unit size, as might be modelled in some packet stream applications, then a schedule must exist as long as the aggregate utilization rate is no more than the number of processors (packet switching resources). Some subclasses of the Window-Constrained Scheduling for unit-size jobs can be transformed to the well known Liu and Layland model or the more recent Pfair model and can therefore be scheduled optimally and at low scheduling cost. In considering the general unit-size-job case, we note that nonproportionate progress in scheduling Window-Constrained tasks is often the cause of unschedulability, no matter how low the aggregate utilization rate is. We shall define the notion of Pfairness in relation to the Window-Constrained Scheduling model so as to quantitatively describe the concept of strictly proportionate progress. An EDF (Earliest-Deadline-First) based algorithm will be dejined for the Window-Constrained Scheduler problem. This algorithm is computationally eficient, on-line, and Pfair: A suficient schedulability test for this EDF-based algorithm is proved.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Advances in computing applications in recent years have prompted the demand for more flexible scheduling models of real-time tasks. A prominent example for this demand is the periodic transmission of audio and video packets. These applications can usually tolerate a short blackout of the packet stream without significantly deteriorating the quality of the audio or video being transmitted. Therefore, when a transmission channel is overloaded, the scheduler may judiciously "skip over" a bounded number of consecutive packets from some video streams. In the periodic realtime task model (commonly known as the Liu and Layland model) proposed in [ 121, if a single entity being scheduled misses its deadline, then the scheduler is considered to In this paper, we shall refer to the entities being scheduled as jobs and tasks, where a task is a sequence of jobs. Beginning from the start time of a task, jobs become ready at the start of fixed intervals.

A real-time task has an (m,k)-firm deadline if at least m out of any IC consecutive jobs from a task must meet their respective deadlines. The scheduling problem of this model has been proved to be NP-hard in the strong sense [14].

However, a number of sub-optimal but computationally efficient algorithms are known and are described in [ 51, [ 101, Window-Constrained scheduling is "easier" than (m,k)firm scheduling: a valid (m,k)-firm schedule must be a valid Window-Constrained schedule, where k is defined to be the size of window and m is the minimum number of jobs to be scheduled in each window; the converse is not necessarily true. This may be seen from the following observation: for Window-Constrained scheduling, if all jobs in a task set have unit-size execution time, then the task set is feasible as long as the total aggregate utilization of the jobs is no more than the total number of processors (packet switching resources), as will be proven later in this paper. The (m,k)-firm scheduling however, does not have this property. The Window-Constrained model is appropriate for applications where the sequence of jobs can be logically divided into segments, and in each segment a minimum number of jobs must be completed. On the other hand, the (m,k)-firm model imposes a minimum job completion requirement on every consecutive IC jobs, regardless whether these jobs are logically related. Thus, the (m,k)-firm model may overspecify the constraints of some applications.

DWCS, which is a scheduling algorithm for the Window-Constrained model, is described in [ 171. Unfortunately, we can show that there exist sets of unit-size Window-Constrained tasks T such that the aggregate utilization of T is arbitrarily low and yet T is not schedulable by DWCS (details follow in Section. 4). In this paper we shall describe a simple scheduling algorithm with a proven worst-case aggregate utilization rate for unit-size tasks.

Related to our research on flexible scheduling is the notion of proportionate progress. Pfairness is a strict proportionate progress property which is quantitatively defined in [4]. There are several optimal and linear algorithms to generate Pfair schedules [2,3,4]. From our experience with the Window-Constrained scheduling problem so far, it seems that Pfaimess is often instrumental in achieving schedulability. We shall define Pfaimess for Window-Constrained model and the schedule produced by the algorithm proposed in this paper is always Pfair.
Our contributions to Window-Constrained Scheduling can be summarized as follows:
We analyze the complexity of the Window-Constrained scheduling problem, from the most general problem to specific sub-classes.
We define Pfaimess quantitatively in relation to Window-Constrained scheduling as a strict form of proportionate progress.
We prove that a Window-Constrained schedule exists if the aggregate utilization rate is no bigger than the number of processors (packet switching resources), for the case of unit-size jobs.
We present a simple, computationally efficient, online, and Pfair scheduling algorithm for the Window-Constrained model, together with a sufficient schedulability condition for this algorithm.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines and explains the Window-Constrained scheduling model, Pfaimess in relation to this model and other important concepts used in this paper. Section 3 proves that Window-Constrained scheduling in general is NP-hard in the strong sense; however, a Pfair Window-Constrained schedule always exists if the execution time of all tasks is of unit-size and the aggregate utilization rate is no more than the total number of processors (packet switching resources). This section also shows that some special cases of Window-Constrained problems can be optimally and efficiently solved. The rest of this paper investigates the Window-Constrained scheduling under the unit-size execution time assumption, because this problem is on the boundary between subclasses with known polynomial online solutions and those without. Section 4 shows the importance of proportionate progress in Window-Constrained scheduling. We show that there exist feasible sets of unitsize Window-Constrained tasks with arbitrarily low aggregate utilization rate that cannot be scheduled by two groups of scheduling algorithms, including DWCS algorithm described in [17]. In Section 5, an EDF (Early-Deadline-First) based scheduling algorithm is defined and a sufficient schedulability test for this algorithm is given. This algorithm is on-line, computationally efficient and Pfair. Section 6 draws conclusions.

div.head: Window-Constrained Scheduling Problems
div.p: Window-Constrained scheduling in general is NP-hard in the strong sense. However, the unit-size Window-Constrained scheduling problem is not NF-hard in the strong sense because there exists a pseudo-polynomial-time optimal algorithm for it. No polynomial-time optimal algorithm for unit-size Window-Constrained scheduling has been found. Some special cases of unit-size scheduling problem can be easily transformed to either periodic task scheduling problem as defined in [I21 or non-Window-Constrained Pfair scheduling problem as defined in [4], and therefore can be optimally and efficiently solved.

Naturally, we want to see whether Window-Constrained scheduling can be solved by an EDF-based on-line algorithm. By EDF, the ready tasks are prioritized according to their deadlines, and the task with the earliest deadline is scheduled first. Therefore, the deadline plays the critical role in scheduling. In this section, we describe two naive approaches to determine deadlines for jobs of Window-Constrained tasks, and use a counter-example to show that both approaches are not optimal because they cause nonproportionate progress among tasks. This section proves that there exist sets of tasks with arbitrarily low aggregate utilization rate but that are unschedulable by either of the two naive approaches. The DWCS algorithm described in [17] is a special case of one of the non-proportionate approaches, and there exists unit-size task sets with arbitrarily low worst-case aggregate utilization rate that can't be scheduled by DWCS as well.

div.p: As has been proved in Sub-section 3.2, a Pfair schedule exists as long as the task set is feasible. The network flow construction in the proof itself indicates an optimal but pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm. In this section, we describe an on-line scheduling algorithm with O ( n . l o g ( n ) ) computational cost. We call this algorithm the EDF based on Pfair scope. The schedule generated by this algorithm is always Pfair. A sufficient schedulability test for this algorithm will be defined and proved.

div.head: The Algorithm
div.p: EDF based on Pfair scope is similar to the approaches proposed in Section 4. However, there are two major differences. First, the ready time of a job to be scheduled must not be earlier than the beginning of its corresponding Pfair scope; second, the deadline of a job to be scheduled is its Pfair scope deadline. This algorithm is formally defined in detail.

The DWCS algorithm was proposed for solving the scheduling problem in RTSS'2000. Unfortunately, we can show that their algorithm is not optimal and in fact may fail for feasible task sets with arbitrarily low aggregate utilization rate, even for unit-size tasks. We summarize the status of the Window-Constrained scheduling problem as follows. In general, Window-Constrained scheduling is NP-hard in the strong sense. Some sub-classes of this model can be scheduled efficiently and optimally. The frontier of research for this model is the unit-size scheduling problem: under the assumption of unit,size execution time, optimal algorithms exist; however, the existence of an optimal and efficient on-line scheduling algorithm remains an open question. We show that non-proportionate progress during scheduling may cause unschedulability, no matter how low the aggregate utilization rate is. We define Pfaimess for the Window-Constrained model to quantitatively express the property of proportionate progress. We define an EDF algorithm based on Pfair scope and we show that this algorithm has several merits. First, its on-line computational cost is O(n.log(n)),

where n represents the number of tasks. Second, the generated schedules are always Pfair, which is a desired feature for some applications. Third, a sufficient but not necessary schedulability test for this algorithm is proved.
